title: Calendaring Standard — First Hearing Date and Notice Period, Unemployment Insurance Appeals
content:
When the appeals office dockets an Unemployment Insurance Appeals appeal filed on a docket that holds hearings, it sets the first hearing by telephone, mails the hearing notice today and notifies every interested party of the docket; the first-setting notice period is the number of calendar days from today, the day the notice is mailed, to the first hearing date. The first hearing date is the date that falls the first-setting target's number of calendar days after the day the first-setting clock starts. The first-setting clock starts on the appeal's filing date. The first-setting target is the docket's scheduling target days. When the first hearing date found this way is fewer than the docket's notice minimum days after today, the first hearing is set the notice minimum days after today instead. A first hearing date that falls on a Saturday or a Sunday moves to the following Monday.

## Structure of the computation

1. **Clock start.** The appeal's filing date, as recorded on the appeal.
2. **Date found.** The filing date moved later by the docket's scheduling target days, counted in calendar days.
3. **Notice minimum.** The date found is compared with today: when it lies fewer than the docket's notice minimum days after today — including when it lies on or before today — the hearing date becomes the date the notice minimum days after today. Otherwise the date found stands. The hearing date is thus the later of the date found and the date the notice minimum days after today.
4. **Weekend.** The date from point 3, if a Saturday, moves 2 days to the following Monday; if a Sunday, 1 day to the following Monday. Any other weekday stands.
5. **Notice period.** The calendar days from today (day 0) to the date from point 4. This whole number is the first-setting notice period.

The notice minimum is applied before the weekend rule, and the notice period is always counted from today, the mailing day of the notice.

## Worked computations (hypothetical inputs: today is Wednesday 15 April 2026; the docket's scheduling target is 30 days or 21 days and its notice minimum 7 days, as stated in each case)

**Case 1 — target 30 days, appeal filed Thursday 2 April 2026.**
Date found: 2 April moved 30 days later is Saturday 2 May, which is 17 days after today. 17 days is not fewer than 7, so 2 May stands. It is a Saturday, so the hearing moves to Monday 4 May. Notice period: from 15 April to 4 May, **19 days**.

**Case 2 — target 21 days, appeal filed Sunday 1 March 2026.**
Date found: 1 March moved 21 days later is Sunday 22 March, 24 days before today. That is fewer than 7 days after today, so the hearing is set 7 days after today, on Wednesday 22 April, a weekday. Notice period: **7 days**.

## Reading points

- Every count here is in calendar days; no business-day count is involved.
- The weekend rule moves a date only forward and only to a Monday.
- The notice minimum compares with *today*, not with the filing date.
